stimuli.title: Iron Across a Continent: Building the First Transcontinental Railroad
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] In the 1850s, a traveler leaving New York for California faced a hard choice. She could spend four to six months crossing the plains and mountains by wagon, or she could go by sea, either sailing all the way around South America or crossing the narrow, disease-ridden Isthmus of Panama. Either way, the trip was expensive, uncomfortable, and dangerous. Many Americans believed that a railroad linking the East to the Pacific coast could tie the growing nation together. For years, however, Congress could not agree on a route, in part because Northern and Southern lawmakers each wanted the line to run through their own region.

[2] The Civil War broke that deadlock. With Southern members gone from Congress, lawmakers passed the Pacific Railway Act, which President Abraham Lincoln signed in July 1862. The law gave the job to two companies. The Central Pacific would build east from Sacramento, California, and the Union Pacific would build west from the Missouri River near Omaha, Nebraska. Because private investors were reluctant to risk money on such an enormous project, the government offered powerful incentives: loans in the form of government bonds for every mile of track completed, with larger amounts for miles laid in hills and mountains, and grants of public land along the route that the companies could sell to settlers.

[3] The Central Pacific faced the harder start. Only about a hundred miles east of Sacramento, its crews had to climb the Sierra Nevada, a wall of granite mountains about 7,000 feet high where the line crossed them. Workers blasted fifteen tunnels through solid rock, sometimes advancing only a foot or so a day. In the winter of 1866–1867, storms buried the work camps under snowdrifts many feet deep, and avalanches swept away men and equipment. The company also struggled to keep laborers, because many quit to search for gold or silver. In 1865, it began hiring Chinese immigrants, at first as an experiment. They proved so skilled and dependable that within a few years they made up the large majority of the Central Pacific’s workforce—by most estimates, more than 10,000 workers. They were paid less than white workers, however, and unlike white workers, they generally had to supply their own food and lodging.

[4] The Union Pacific crossed easier ground, the open grasslands of the Great Plains, but it had challenges of its own. Its crews, many of them Irish immigrants and veterans of both the Union and Confederate armies, had to haul nearly every rail, tie, and spike hundreds of miles across country with few trees. The line also cut through the homelands of the Lakota, Cheyenne, and other Plains nations, who had never agreed to it. As conflicts grew, the army sent troops to protect the work crews.

[5] As the two lines drew closer, the companies raced each other, because every mile of track brought more bonds and more land. On one April day in 1869, a Central Pacific crew laid ten miles of track, a record for track laid by hand in a single day. Finally, on May 10, 1869, the two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory. A ceremonial golden spike was tapped into place, and a telegraph operator sent a one-word message to a waiting nation: “DONE.”

[6] The results were dramatic. A trip from coast to coast that had taken months now took about a week. Settlers poured west, towns sprang up along the tracks, and farmers and ranchers could ship crops and cattle to distant markets. Yet the railroad’s benefits were not shared equally. Easier travel brought hunters who slaughtered the bison herds on which many Plains nations depended, and the flood of settlers pushed Native peoples onto ever-smaller reservations. Meanwhile, in 1872, newspapers revealed that Union Pacific insiders had used a construction company called Crédit Mobilier to overcharge for the work and had handed out shares to members of Congress, one of the great political scandals of the century.

[7] Today, the transcontinental railroad is often remembered through the image of the golden spike. But the spike was removed soon after the ceremony. What remained were the miles of track, built by thousands of workers whose names few people recorded, and a nation that would never again be as far apart as it once had been.

stimuli.title: The Color of the Kitchen
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] At 5:40 on a Saturday, twenty minutes before closing, the paint counter at Hadley’s Hardware was the quietest place in the store. Dana had already wiped down the tinting machine, capped the colorant nozzles, and stacked the stir sticks in their cup like pencils. In her mind she was halfway out the door when the old man set a small envelope on the counter.

[2] “I need this,” he said. “Exactly this.”

[3] Inside was a chip of paint no bigger than a postage stamp, yellow, with a curl of older green clinging to its back. Dana turned it over with a fingernail. “Where’s it from?”

[4] “Behind the refrigerator. Only place the sun never got to.” He cleared his throat. “My wife picked it out. Nineteen eighty-one. I’ve been meaning to repaint the kitchen, and I’d like it to look the way it did.”

[5] Dana nodded the way she nodded at every customer, pleasant and quick. She set the chip under the scanner’s eye, and in a few seconds the screen produced a formula: a base, four colorants, every drop measured to the hundredth. The machine hummed and dispensed, and she clamped a sample quart into the shaker. The whole thing rattled like a washing machine with a shoe in it. Five minutes, she thought. Six at most.

[6] She brushed a stripe of the new paint onto a card, dried it with the heat gun, and laid the chip beside it. They were not the same. The stripe was right in the way a photograph of a person is right: it had all the correct parts. But next to the chip it looked thin and a little cold, like a lemon pretending to be butter.

[7] “Close,” she said, which was what Walt, the old paint manager, used to call a lie with good manners.

[8] The man bent over the card. He did not say anything for a long moment. Then he said, “Close,” too, and she heard what it cost him.

[9] Walt had retired in the spring. On her first day, he had told her that the scanner saw color the way a calculator sees money: it got the numbers right and missed the point. “Light changes everything,” he had said. “You’ve got to look at a color where it’s going to live.” She had written that off as the kind of thing old men say.

[10] Dana glanced at the clock. 5:52. She reached for the colorant dial.

[11] She added a drop of red oxide, shook, brushed, dried. Too orange. She started over with a fresh quart and added a whisper of raw umber instead. Better, but now it was muddy. She carried the card and the chip to the front window, where the last of the afternoon sun slanted in over the sacks of birdseed, and held them side by side. The man followed her without being asked.

[12] At 6:10 the store manager switched off the overhead lights in the garden aisle and looked pointedly at Dana. She held up one finger.

[13] The fourth try was the one. In the window light, the stripe and the chip seemed to lean toward each other. It still wasn’t perfect. There was something in the old paint, forty years of steam from soup pots and the breath of people talking over coffee, that no colorant could add.

[14] “It’s still not exact,” she admitted.

[15] The man smiled for the first time. “It never was one color anyway. In the morning it was butter. By supper it was almost orange. Ruth used to say those walls kept better time than the clock did.” He tapped the card. “This is right.”

[16] Dana mixed two gallons. When she hammered the lids down, she took a marker and wrote the formula across the top of each can, the way Walt always had, so it could be made again. Then, under the numbers, without quite deciding to, she wrote a name: Ruth’s Kitchen.

[17] He read it, and nodded, and carried the cans out into the evening, one in each hand, walking slowly, as if they were full of something that might spill.

stimuli.title: Draft Policy: Shift Scheduling at The Saffron Table
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
The following restaurant policy is a first draft. Numbered blanks mark places that need editing. Answer the questions that follow.

To: All Staff, The Saffron Table
From: Rosa Delgado, General Manager
Subject: Updated Shift Scheduling Policy

Beginning May 1, The Saffron Table will follow a new scheduling policy. Its goal is to make schedules more predictable and to treat every team member fairly.

Posting the schedule. The weekly schedule for all servers, hosts, and kitchen staff (1) posted every Thursday by noon. It covers the following Monday through Sunday. Please check it as soon as it is posted, because you are responsible for knowing your shifts. Servers and hosts should also confirm (2) section assignments with the shift lead before each shift, since large parties sometimes book at the last minute.

Time off. Requests for time off must be entered in the scheduling app before the schedule is posted(3) submitted after that are approved only if the shift can be covered. (4), managers will always make exceptions for medical and family emergencies.

Shift swaps. You may trade a shift with a coworker who is trained for the same position. Both employees must sign a swap form, and a manager must approve it at least 24 hours before the shift. Send the completed form to Assistant Manager Kenji Tran or (5).

Weekend fairness. Reviewing everyone’s availability each week, (6) so that no one works every Friday and Saturday night.

Holidays. During our busiest holidays, such as (7), all staff should expect to work at least one shift.

Attendance. Employees who arrive late, leave early without permission, or (8) will receive a written warning.

Leaving the team. If you plan to leave The Saffron Table, please give at least two (9) notice so that we can adjust the schedule.

stimuli.title: A Bag Ban Is a Simple Step Toward a Cleaner Corliss Falls
stimuli.source: By Teresa Nwosu, member of the Corliss Falls Conservation Commission. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Every year, the volunteers who clean the banks of the Sable River pull out the same thing over and over: plastic shopping bags. The bags snag in branches, wrap around fishing line, and slowly break into small pieces that never truly disappear. Corliss Falls should join the growing number of communities that have banned single-use plastic shopping bags at checkout.

The best evidence comes from our neighbor. In 2022, the town of Easton Ridge banned thin plastic bags and required stores to charge 10 cents for each paper bag. Volunteers there have counted litter at the same cleanup sites, using the same method, every spring. In the spring before the ban, they collected 1,240 plastic bags. Two years later, they collected 310, a drop of 75 percent. Over the same period, the total amount of other litter they collected stayed about the same, which suggests that the ban, not a smaller cleanup effort, made the difference.

The fee on paper bags matters as much as the ban itself. Without a fee, shoppers simply switch to paper, which takes more energy and water to produce. With one, they change their habits. Easton Ridge’s two largest grocery stores reported that within a year, about 6 in 10 customers were bringing their own bags. A sturdy bag that is reused dozens of times does far less harm than any single-use bag, paper or plastic.

Opponents say a ban hurts families on tight budgets. That concern is real, and a good policy should address it. Easton Ridge waived the paper-bag fee for customers paying with food assistance benefits and gave away more than 4,000 free reusable bags through its food pantry and senior center. Corliss Falls can do the same.

Some people say plastic bags are too small a problem to bother with. But a bag ban is one of the rare environmental policies that costs taxpayers almost nothing and asks residents only to change a habit. And anyone who has seen a heron tangled in a plastic bag knows the problem is not small to the animals that live along our river.

Corliss Falls has the chance to keep the Sable River cleaner with a simple, proven step. The town council should pass the ban this spring.

stimuli.title: Bag Ban Is the Wrong Answer for Corliss Falls
stimuli.source: By Dale Kowalczyk, owner of Kowalczyk’s Family Market. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
I have run a grocery store in Corliss Falls for twenty-two years, and I care about the Sable River as much as anyone. But banning plastic shopping bags would raise costs for local businesses and shoppers while doing little for the environment.

Start with the cost. My store gives out about 6,000 bags a week. A plastic bag costs me about 3 cents; a paper bag costs about 12 cents. Switching to paper would add more than $500 a week to my costs, or about $28,000 a year. A small store like mine cannot absorb that. The big chain stores out on Route 9 can, and they will gladly take my customers when I am forced to raise prices.

Supporters say a fee on paper bags will solve this, but a fee is just another tax on shoppers. Families who are already stretching every dollar at the checkout will pay the most.

Paper is not the green choice it seems, either. Studies have shown that making a paper bag uses far more energy and water than making a plastic one, and paper bags are heavier to truck. A ban could actually make things worse.

Plastic bags also are not “single-use” in most homes. My customers tell me they use them to line trash cans, pick up after their dogs, and pack lunches. If the town bans them, people will just buy boxes of thicker plastic bags for those jobs. One customer told me she has not thrown away a grocery bag in ten years.

Besides, plastic bags are a tiny share of litter. According to one national survey, they make up less than 1 percent of the litter items found along roadsides. If we want a cleaner river, we should put more trash cans along the river trail and fine people who litter, instead of punishing everyone for the actions of a few.

Finally, where does this end? Today it is shopping bags. Tomorrow the council will ban takeout containers, then straws, then anything else someone finds on a riverbank. The people of Corliss Falls are capable of making their own choices.

Let the market and personal responsibility do their work. The council should vote no on the bag ban.

stimuli.title: Draft Letter to the Editor: Keep the Summer Youth Crew
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
The following letter to the editor is a first draft. Numbered blanks mark places that need editing. Answer the questions that follow.

To the Editor:

Last week, the Westbury City Council proposed eliminating the parks department’s Summer Youth Crew to help close a budget gap. I am writing to urge council members to reconsider. Over the past eight years, the program has proven (1) value many times over.

Each summer, the program hires about thirty local teenagers. The crew members, who are between sixteen and eighteen years old, (2) trails, paint picnic shelters, and plant trees in parks across the city. The cost of the crew’s wages, tools, and supplies (3) less than $90,000 a year, a small share of the city’s budget.

The work also has a lasting (4) on the teenagers who do it. Last summer, my daughter (5) on the crew that rebuilt the boardwalk at Willow Pond. She had never used a power drill before June. (6), by August she was teaching new crew members how to use one safely. Crew members also receive reference letters from their supervisors, which (7) can use when they apply for jobs or college.

Cutting the program would save money this year(8) it would cost the community much more in the long run. I hope every council member will visit Willow Pond this summer and see what these young people have built.

Sincerely,
Linda Morales
Westbury

stimuli.title: From Lab to Pharmacy: How New Medicines Are Tested
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] Before a new medicine reaches a pharmacy shelf, it usually goes through years of testing. Most of that testing happens in clinical trials, carefully planned studies in which volunteers take an experimental treatment so that researchers can learn whether it is safe and whether it works. Clinical trials are slow and expensive, and most experimental drugs that enter them never reach patients. Yet trials remain the most reliable method scientists have for separating treatments that truly help from those that only seem to.

[2] Testing begins long before any person takes a new drug. In laboratory and animal studies, researchers look for signs that a compound might be effective and for evidence that it might be harmful. Only a compound that passes these early tests can move on to studies in people, and in the United States, researchers must first submit their plans to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

[3] Clinical trials are usually conducted in phases. Phase 1 trials involve a small group of volunteers, often fewer than 100 people, and focus mainly on safety: what dose people can take, how the body processes the drug, and what side effects appear. Phase 2 trials enroll up to several hundred people who have the condition the drug is meant to treat; these studies look for early signs that the drug works while continuing to watch for side effects. Phase 3 trials are the largest, often including several hundred to several thousand participants. They compare the new drug with a placebo or with the best treatment already available. If the results show that the benefits outweigh the risks, the company can ask the FDA for approval. Even after approval, monitoring continues, because rare side effects may appear only after many thousands of people have used a drug.

[4] Several design features protect the results from bias. In a randomized trial, a computer program assigns each participant to a group by chance, so that the groups end up alike in age, health, and other traits. If doctors chose who received the new drug, they might, even without meaning to, give it to healthier patients, making the drug look more effective than it is. Many trials are also “double-blind”: neither the participants nor the researchers who measure the results know who is receiving the real drug. This matters because expectations can shape results. Patients who believe they are taking a promising new medicine sometimes report feeling better even when they have been given a placebo, a harmless pill with no active ingredient. This placebo effect is one reason a trial must compare the new drug with a control group rather than simply giving it to patients and seeing whether they improve.

[5] Protecting volunteers is as important as producing good data. Before joining a trial, each person must give informed consent: researchers must explain the study’s purpose, its procedures, its possible risks and benefits, and the person’s right to leave the study at any time. An independent review board must approve the study before it begins, and in many larger trials a separate safety board reviews the data while the trial is under way. If one group is clearly being harmed, or clearly benefiting, the board can recommend stopping the trial early.

[6] Clinical trials also face a long-standing problem: the people who volunteer do not always reflect the people who will eventually use the drug. For decades, many trials enrolled mostly white men, and women who could become pregnant were often excluded. Older adults, who take more medicines than any other age group, have also frequently been left out. Because age, sex, and other factors can affect how a body responds to a drug, results from a narrow group of volunteers may not apply to everyone. In recent years, regulators and researchers have pushed trials to recruit more diverse participants, for example by opening study sites in more neighborhoods and reducing the number of required visits.

[7] The process is demanding, and critics argue that it can delay treatments that patients urgently need. For serious diseases with few options, the FDA has created faster pathways that allow some drugs to be approved on the basis of earlier evidence, with further study required afterward. Still, the basic logic of the clinical trial has held up for good reason. A medicine that may be taken by millions of people should be judged not by hope or by a handful of success stories, but by careful comparison.

stimuli.title: Volunteer Information Sheet: Study LMR-214
stimuli.source: Original document written for KCE GED Prep. The study and medicine are fictional.
stimuli.html:
Lakeshore Medical Research Center
A Study of an Experimental Medicine for High Blood Pressure

Why is this study being done?

Researchers want to learn whether an experimental medicine called LX-7 lowers blood pressure in adults who have high blood pressure, and to watch for any side effects. An earlier study in 60 healthy volunteers found the doses used in this study to be safe for short-term use. LX-7 has not been approved by the FDA.

Who can join?

About 240 adults will take part. You may be able to join if you

  • are 30 to 75 years old,
  • have been diagnosed with high blood pressure, and
  • take no more than one blood pressure medicine.

You cannot join if you are pregnant or have kidney disease.

What will happen?

The study lasts 12 weeks and includes 6 visits to our clinic. A computer will assign you by chance to one of two groups. One group will take LX-7; the other will take a placebo, a pill that looks the same but contains no medicine. You will have an equal chance of being placed in either group. Neither you nor the study staff will know which pill you are taking until the study ends. You will also check your blood pressure at home each morning with a monitor we provide.

What are the possible risks and benefits?

In the earlier study, the most common side effects were mild headaches and dizziness. There may be risks that are not yet known. Taking part may or may not improve your blood pressure. What researchers learn may help other people with high blood pressure in the future.

Will I be paid?

You will receive $50 for each completed clinic visit, and parking is free.

What are my rights?

Taking part is your choice. You may leave the study at any time, for any reason. Leaving will not affect the care you receive from your own doctor. Before you join, a study nurse will go over this information with you and answer your questions, and you will be asked to sign a consent form.

Questions? Call the study office Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The transcontinental railroad was finished quickly because the Central Pacific and Union Pacific raced each other to collect government bonds.
Building the railroad was more difficult in the Sierra Nevada than on the Great Plains, mainly because of snow and solid granite.
Made possible by government support and the labor of thousands of workers, the railroad transformed the nation, though its costs and benefits fell unevenly.
The golden spike remains the most important symbol of the transcontinental railroad because it marked the moment the nation was joined.
items.explain:
The passage moves from why the railroad was wanted and how the government funded it (paragraphs 1–2), to the workers who built it (paragraphs 3–5), to its effects, both the benefits and the harms to Plains nations, plus the Crédit Mobilier scandal (paragraph 6). Only the statement about government support, the workers, and the uneven costs and benefits covers all of this.

The race between companies (paragraph 5) and the Sierra Nevada hardships (paragraph 3) are supporting details. Paragraph 7 actually downplays the golden spike, noting it was removed and that the track and workers are what lasted.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 2.

“The Civil War broke that deadlock.”

As used in the passage, deadlock means
options: a locked gate that blocks a route
a disagreement that keeps any action from being taken
a violent conflict between two regions
a shortage of money for a large project
items.explain:
“That deadlock” refers back to the end of paragraph 1: “For years, however, Congress could not agree on a route.” The two sides were stuck, so nothing happened. When Southern members left Congress, the stalemate ended and the law passed.

The Civil War itself was a violent conflict, but the word deadlock names the situation the war ended, not the war. Money problems are discussed later and are not what was “broken.”

items.prompt: Part of paragraph 3 is shown below. Click the sentence that shows Chinese workers were treated unequally compared with other workers.
spans: The company also struggled to keep laborers, because many quit to search for gold or silver.
In 1865, it began hiring Chinese immigrants, at first as an experiment.
They proved so skilled and dependable that within a few years they made up the large majority of the Central Pacific’s workforce—by most estimates, more than 10,000 workers.
They were paid less than white workers, however, and unlike white workers, they generally had to supply their own food and lodging.
items.explain:
The last sentence directly compares the Chinese workers with white workers: they were “paid less” and “had to supply their own food and lodging.” That is unequal treatment.

The sentence about the workers being “skilled and dependable” praises them; it says nothing about how they were treated.

items.prompt: The passage describes the railroad from its approval in Congress to the scandal that followed its completion. Arrange these five railroad events in chronological order by dragging each one into the correct position.
choices: A crew lays ten miles of track in a single day.
Newspapers reveal the Crédit Mobilier scandal.
President Lincoln signs the Pacific Railway Act.
The two lines meet at Promontory Summit.
The Central Pacific begins hiring Chinese immigrants.
items.explain: (1) Lincoln signs the Pacific Railway Act in July 1862 (paragraph 2). (2) The Central Pacific begins hiring Chinese immigrants in 1865 (paragraph 3). (3) A crew lays ten miles of track on one April day in 1869 (paragraph 5). (4) The lines meet at Promontory Summit on May 10, 1869 (paragraph 5). (5) The Crédit Mobilier scandal is revealed in 1872 (paragraph 6).

items.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the government most likely offer larger loans for track laid in hills and mountains?
options: Mountain land was more valuable to sell to settlers than land on the plains.
The Union Pacific needed extra money to protect its crews from conflicts on the Great Plains.
Congress wanted the Central Pacific to finish its section before the Union Pacific did.
Building through mountains was slower and more costly than building across flat land.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 shows why mountain miles cost more: crews “blasted fifteen tunnels through solid rock, sometimes advancing only a foot or so a day,” and faced deep snow and avalanches. Larger loans for these miles would cover the greater cost and difficulty.

The passage never says mountain land was more valuable, and the army, not the loans, protected Union Pacific crews. Nothing suggests Congress favored one company.

items.prompt: How does the information in paragraph 5 about the companies racing each other connect to paragraph 2?
options: It shows that the government incentives described in paragraph 2 shaped how the companies behaved.
It shows that the Pacific Railway Act described in paragraph 2 was passed too quickly.
It contradicts paragraph 2’s claim that private investors were reluctant to fund the project.
It explains why Northern and Southern lawmakers could not agree on a route.
items.explain:
Paragraph 2 says the government gave bonds “for every mile of track completed” and land along the route. Paragraph 5 says the companies raced “because every mile of track brought more bonds and more land.” The race is a direct result of those incentives.

The race does not contradict the investors’ reluctance; the incentives were offered because of it. The route dispute was settled before the race began.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, the author states that “the railroad’s benefits were not shared equally.” Which details best support this claim? Select two answers.
options: A trip from coast to coast took about a week instead of months.
Farmers and ranchers could ship crops and cattle to distant markets.
Hunters slaughtered the bison herds on which many Plains nations depended.
The flood of settlers pushed Native peoples onto ever-smaller reservations.
A telegraph operator sent the message “DONE” to the nation.
A crew laid ten miles of track in a single day.
items.explain:
The claim is that some groups did not benefit. The destruction of the bison herds and the loss of Native land to reservations show the railroad harming Plains nations while it helped others.

Faster travel and new markets are benefits, not evidence of unequal sharing. The telegraph message and the ten-mile day describe the building of the railroad, not its results.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 7?
options: to explain why the golden spike was taken away after the ceremony
to argue that the transcontinental railroad should not be celebrated
to suggest that the workers and the lasting track matter more than the ceremony’s famous symbol
to describe how the railroad is used today
items.explain:
The author contrasts the famous image of the golden spike, which “was removed soon after the ceremony,” with what “remained”: the track “built by thousands of workers whose names few people recorded” and a more connected nation. The point is that the real legacy is the work, not the symbol.

The paragraph does not explain why the spike was removed, does not reject celebrating the railroad, and says nothing about how the railroad is used today.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 1 and 5, how does Dana first approach the old man’s request?
options: She doubts that the paint chip came from his kitchen.
She treats it as a routine task she hopes to finish before closing.
She is annoyed that he arrived so close to closing time.
She worries that the scanner will not be able to read such a small chip.
items.explain:
Before he arrives, Dana is “halfway out the door” in her mind (paragraph 1). She nods “the way she nodded at every customer, pleasant and quick,” and thinks, “Five minutes ... Six at most” (paragraph 5). She sees the job as ordinary and quick.

Her nod is “pleasant,” so she is not shown as annoyed, and she never questions the chip’s origin or the scanner’s ability. She trusts the machine at first.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, the new paint is described as looking “like a lemon pretending to be butter.” What does this comparison suggest?
options: The new color is a sharper, cooler imitation that lacks the warmth of the original.
The new paint is too thick and will be difficult to brush onto a wall.
The original kitchen color was a pale shade of green.
Dana believes the old man is pretending to remember the color.
items.explain:
The same sentence says the stripe “looked thin and a little cold” next to the chip. A lemon is a sharp, sour yellow; butter is a soft, warm one. The comparison shows that the new paint copies the color without its warmth.

“Thin” describes how the color looks, not how thick the paint is. The green is an older layer on the back of the chip, not the kitchen color the man wants.

items.prompt: Paragraph 11 is shown below. Click the sentence that shows Dana beginning to follow Walt’s advice.
spans: She added a drop of red oxide, shook, brushed, dried.
She started over with a fresh quart and added a whisper of raw umber instead.
Better, but now it was muddy.
She carried the card and the chip to the front window, where the last of the afternoon sun slanted in over the sacks of birdseed, and held them side by side.
The man followed her without being asked.
items.explain:
Walt told Dana that “light changes everything” and that she had to look at a color in the light where it will be used (paragraph 9). When she carries the card and chip to the window to compare them in natural sunlight, she is acting on that advice.

Adding red oxide or raw umber is adjusting the formula, which Dana would do with or without Walt’s advice about light.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Older workers usually know more than the machines that replace them.
It is better to follow a careful formula than to rely on your own judgment.
People should let go of the past instead of trying to bring it back.
Care and close attention can capture what matters about something, even when an exact copy is impossible.
items.explain:
The final paint “still wasn’t perfect” (paragraph 13), yet the man says, “This is right” (paragraph 15). Dana’s extra effort, testing in real light and staying past closing, captures the feeling of Ruth’s kitchen even though no colorant can reproduce “forty years of steam.”

The story does not reject the past; the man does recreate his kitchen. The machine’s formula is what fails at first, so the statement that it is better to follow a careful formula reverses the story’s message. Walt’s advice matters, but the story is not a general claim that older workers beat machines.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 8.

“Then he said, ‘Close,’ too, and she heard what it cost him.”

What does this sentence suggest about the old man?
options: He is worried about how much the paint will cost.
He thinks Dana has not tried hard enough.
He is disappointed but is trying to be polite.
He cannot see the difference between the two colors.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 explains that “Close” is “a lie with good manners.” When the man repeats the word after a long silence, he is accepting the match politely, and Dana can hear that doing so hurts him. “Cost” here means an emotional cost, not money.

He bends over the card and studies it, so he does see the difference. He does not blame Dana.

items.prompt: Which details show that Dana’s attitude toward the job has changed by the end of the story? Select two answers.
options: She stacks the stir sticks in their cup like pencils.
She nods “pleasant and quick” when the man explains his request.
She thinks the job will take five or six minutes.
She holds up one finger when the manager signals that the store is closing.
She writes the name Ruth’s Kitchen on the paint cans.
She sets the chip under the scanner’s eye.
items.explain:
At first Dana wants to finish quickly. By the end she asks the manager for more time after closing (holding up one finger at 6:10) and, “without quite deciding to,” names the paint after the man’s wife. Both show she has come to care about the request.

Stacking stir sticks, the quick nod, the five-minute estimate, and using the scanner all come from the beginning of the story, before her attitude changes.

items.prompt: Why does the author include Walt’s comparison of the scanner to a calculator in paragraph 9?
options: to show that Walt did not trust new technology in the store
to set up the idea that exact measurement alone cannot capture what matters about a color
to explain why the store manager wants Dana to close on time
to suggest that Dana is better at math than at mixing paint
items.explain:
Walt says the scanner “got the numbers right and missed the point.” This prepares the reader for what happens next: the machine’s formula has “all the correct parts” but looks wrong, and Dana succeeds only by looking at the color in real light. The comparison introduces the story’s central contrast between precision and perception.

Walt still used formulas (he wrote them on every lid), so he is not shown rejecting technology. The comparison has nothing to do with the manager or Dana’s math skills.

items.prompt: In paragraph 15, the man says, “Ruth used to say those walls kept better time than the clock did.” What does this suggest?
options: The kitchen’s color changed with the light through the day, and Ruth noticed and enjoyed it.
The kitchen clock in the man’s house was often broken.
Ruth chose the yellow paint because it matched the kitchen clock.
The man is in a hurry to get home and begin painting.
items.explain:
Just before this line, the man says the kitchen “was butter” in the morning and “almost orange” by supper. Because the color shifted with the sunlight, a person could tell the time of day by looking at the walls. Ruth’s saying shows she paid loving attention to this.

Nothing in the story says a clock was broken or that the paint matched a clock, and the man walks out “slowly,” not in a hurry.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The weekly schedule for all servers, hosts, and kitchen staff {{0}} posted every Thursday by noon.”

options: are
is
were
have been

items.explain:
The subject is schedule, which is singular. The phrase “for all servers, hosts, and kitchen staff” comes between the subject and the verb but does not change it. A singular subject needs a singular verb: is.

“Are,” “were,” and “have been” are plural verbs that agree with “staff” or the list, not with the true subject. “Were” is also the wrong tense for a regular weekly event.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Servers and hosts should also confirm {{0}} section assignments with the shift lead before each shift, since large parties sometimes book at the last minute.”

options: there
they’re
their
there’s

items.explain:
The sentence needs a possessive word showing whose section assignments: the servers’ and hosts’. Their is the possessive pronoun.

“There” refers to a place, “they’re” means “they are,” and “there’s” means “there is.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Requests for time off must be entered in the scheduling app before the schedule is posted{{0}} submitted after that are approved only if the shift can be covered.”

options: , requests
requests
; and requests
. Requests

items.explain:
Both parts are complete sentences: “Requests ... must be entered ... before the schedule is posted” and “Requests submitted after that are approved only if ...” Separating them with a period creates two correct sentences.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation creates a run-on. A semicolon followed by “and” is incorrect; a semicolon replaces the conjunction rather than joining with it.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“{{0}}, managers will always make exceptions for medical and family emergencies.”

options: However
Therefore
For example
Similarly

items.explain:
The previous sentence sets a strict rule: late requests are approved only if the shift can be covered. This sentence presents an exception to that rule, which is a contrast. However signals contrast.

“Therefore” signals a result, “For example” introduces an illustration, and “Similarly” signals a comparison. None fits an exception.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Send the completed form to Assistant Manager Kenji Tran or {{0}}.”

options: I
myself
me
mine

items.explain:
The pronoun is an object of the preposition “to” (send it to Kenji Tran or to ___). Objects take the objective case: me. Test it by removing the other name: “Send the completed form to me.”

“I” is a subject pronoun. “Myself” is reflexive and is used only when the subject is also “I.” “Mine” shows possession.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Reviewing everyone’s availability each week, {{0}} so that no one works every Friday and Saturday night.”

options: weekend shifts are rotated by the managers
the managers rotate weekend shifts
the rotation of weekend shifts is planned
the schedule rotates weekend shifts

items.explain:
An introductory phrase describes the subject that comes right after the comma. The people who are “reviewing everyone’s availability” are the managers, so the managers must come next.

The other choices make “weekend shifts,” “the rotation,” or “the schedule” the subject, which creates a dangling modifier; shifts and schedules cannot review anyone’s availability.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“During our busiest holidays, such as {{0}}, all staff should expect to work at least one shift.”

options: mother’s day and new year’s eve
Mother’s day and New Year’s eve
mother’s Day and new Year’s Eve
Mother’s Day and New Year’s Eve

items.explain:
The names of holidays are proper nouns, so every main word is capitalized: Mother’s Day and New Year’s Eve.

The other choices leave at least one word of a holiday name lowercase.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Employees who arrive late, leave early without permission, or {{0}} will receive a written warning.”

options: missing a shift without notice
a shift is missed without notice
miss a shift without notice
have been missing shifts without notice

items.explain:
The items in the series must have the same form. The first two are present-tense verb phrases: “arrive late” and “leave early.” The third should match: miss a shift without notice.

“Missing” is an -ing form, “a shift is missed” is a separate clause in the passive voice, and “have been missing” changes the tense, so none is parallel.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the restaurant policy. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you plan to leave The Saffron Table, please give at least two {{0}} notice so that we can adjust the schedule.”

options: weeks
weeks’
week’s
weeks’s

items.explain:
The notice belongs to (is the length of) two weeks, so the plural noun weeks needs a possessive apostrophe. For a plural noun ending in -s, add only the apostrophe: weeks’ notice (compare “one week’s notice”).

“Weeks” has no apostrophe, “week’s” is singular, and “weeks’s” adds an extra s.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of a proposed ban on single-use plastic shopping bags in the town of Corliss Falls.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Over the past eight years, the program has proven {{0}} value many times over.”

options: it’s
its’
their
its

items.explain:
The sentence needs a possessive pronoun for “the program”: the value belongs to the program. Its (no apostrophe) is the possessive form of “it.”

“It’s” means “it is” or “it has.” “Its’” is not a word. “Their” is plural and does not agree with the singular “program.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The crew members, who are between sixteen and eighteen years old, {{0}} trails, paint picnic shelters, and plant trees in parks across the city.”

options: clear
clearing
who clear
to clear

items.explain:
The subject “The crew members” needs a main verb. “Who are between sixteen and eighteen years old” is only a describing clause. Clear supplies the main verb and is parallel with “paint” and “plant.”

“Clearing,” “who clear,” and “to clear” cannot serve as a main verb, so each would leave the sentence a fragment.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The cost of the crew’s wages, tools, and supplies {{0}} less than $90,000 a year, a small share of the city’s budget.”

options: are
were
is
have been

items.explain:
The subject is cost, which is singular. “Of the crew’s wages, tools, and supplies” is a prepositional phrase and does not affect the verb. The letter describes a current yearly amount, so use the singular present: is.

“Are,” “were,” and “have been” are plural forms that wrongly agree with “supplies.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The work also has a lasting {{0}} on the teenagers who do it.”

options: affect
effect
affects
effects

items.explain:
After “a lasting,” the sentence needs a singular noun. Effect is the noun meaning “a result or influence.”

“Affect” and “affects” are usually verbs meaning “to influence.” “Effects” is plural and does not fit with the article “a.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Last summer, my daughter {{0}} on the crew that rebuilt the boardwalk at Willow Pond.”

options: works
will work
has been working
worked

items.explain:
“Last summer” places the action in the finished past, and the rest of the sentence uses the past tense (“rebuilt”). The simple past worked is correct.

“Works” is present, “will work” is future, and “has been working” suggests the action is still going on.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“She had never used a power drill before June. {{0}}, by August she was teaching new crew members how to use one safely.”

options: As a result
In addition
Yet
In other words

items.explain:
The two sentences contrast: she had no experience in June, but she was teaching others by August. Yet signals that surprising contrast.

“As a result” would mean her lack of experience caused her to teach. “In addition” simply adds information, and “In other words” restates an idea; neither shows contrast.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Crew members also receive reference letters from their supervisors, which {{0}} can use when they apply for jobs or college.”

options: they
it
he
you

items.explain:
The pronoun refers to “crew members,” a plural noun, and later in the sentence the writer uses “they apply.” The plural pronoun they agrees.

“It” and “he” are singular. “You” shifts to the second person, addressing the reader instead of describing the crew members.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the letter to the editor. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Cutting the program would save money this year{{0}} it would cost the community much more in the long run.”

options: , however
, but
so

items.explain:
The sentence joins two complete thoughts that contrast: the cut would save money now but cost more later. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction but joins them correctly and shows the contrast.

“However” is not a coordinating conjunction, so “, however” creates a comma splice, as does a comma alone. “So” without a comma creates a run-on and wrongly signals a result.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Clinical trials take so long that they often delay treatments patients urgently need.
Most experimental drugs fail during clinical trials because of their side effects.
The placebo effect makes it nearly impossible to know whether a new drug really works.
Although slow and imperfect, carefully designed clinical trials are the most reliable way to learn whether new medicines are safe and effective.
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 states that trials “remain the most reliable method” for telling helpful treatments apart, and the rest of the passage explains how phases, randomization, blinding, and consent make them reliable and safe. The author also admits problems (diversity, delays) but concludes that the “basic logic of the clinical trial has held up for good reason.”

Delays are a criticism the author mentions and answers, not the central idea. The passage never says most drugs fail because of side effects, and it presents the placebo effect as something trials are designed to account for, not an impossible obstacle.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 4, what problem does random assignment help prevent?
options: Volunteers might drop out of the study before it ends.
Doctors might give the new drug to healthier patients, making it look more effective than it is.
Researchers might not recruit enough participants to reach a conclusion.
Patients might feel better simply because they believe they are taking a new medicine.
items.explain:
The passage says that if doctors chose who received the drug, “they might, even without meaning to, give it to healthier patients, making the drug look more effective than it is.” Assigning people by chance keeps the groups alike.

Patients feeling better because of their beliefs is the placebo effect, which the passage connects to blinding and control groups, not randomization. Dropouts and recruitment are not discussed in paragraph 4.

items.prompt: Part of paragraph 4 is shown below. Click the sentence that gives an example of how expectations can shape the results of a trial.
spans: Many trials are also “double-blind”: neither the participants nor the researchers who measure the results know who is receiving the real drug.
This matters because expectations can shape results.
Patients who believe they are taking a promising new medicine sometimes report feeling better even when they have been given a placebo, a harmless pill with no active ingredient.
This placebo effect is one reason a trial must compare the new drug with a control group rather than simply giving it to patients and seeing whether they improve.
items.explain:
The third sentence gives a specific example: patients who believe they are getting a new medicine “report feeling better” even on a placebo. Their expectation changes the result.

The second sentence states the general idea (“expectations can shape results”) but gives no example. The fourth sentence explains a consequence for trial design.

items.prompt: Based on paragraph 3, match each description to the phase of clinical trials it describes. Drag each description into the correct box.
choices: Often fewer than 100 volunteers, focusing mainly on safety
Studies how the body processes the drug and what dose people can take
Up to several hundred people with the condition; looks for early signs the drug works
Several hundred to several thousand participants
Compares the drug with a placebo or the best existing treatment before the company seeks approval
items.explain:
Phase 1: a small group, “often fewer than 100 people,” focused on safety, including “what dose people can take” and “how the body processes the drug.”

Phase 2: “up to several hundred people who have the condition,” looking for “early signs that the drug works.”

Phase 3: “several hundred to several thousand participants,” comparing the drug “with a placebo or with the best treatment already available,” after which the company can seek FDA approval.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from paragraph 6.

“Clinical trials also face a long-standing problem: the people who volunteer do not always reflect the people who will eventually use the drug.”

As used in this sentence, reflect means
options: think carefully about
send back light from
accurately represent
show approval of
items.explain:
The paragraph goes on to explain that trial volunteers were mostly white men while many other groups who use medicines were left out. The volunteers did not accurately represent, or match, the people who would use the drug.

“Think carefully about” and “send back light” are other meanings of reflect that do not fit this context, and nothing in the sentence concerns approval.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 7?
options: to acknowledge a criticism of clinical trials and explain why the author still supports them
to argue that the FDA should approve all drugs for serious diseases more quickly
to show that success stories are better evidence than careful comparison
to describe the steps a company follows after a drug is approved
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 opens with a criticism: trials “can delay treatments that patients urgently need.” It notes the faster pathways the FDA created, then concludes, “Still, the basic logic of the clinical trial has held up for good reason.” This is a concession followed by a response.

The author does not call for approving all drugs faster, and explicitly says medicines should be judged by careful comparison, not “a handful of success stories.” Post-approval monitoring appears in paragraph 3, not 7.

items.prompt: A new arthritis drug was tested only on volunteers ages 25 to 45. Based on paragraph 6, what is the most reasonable concern about this trial?
options: The trial could not have been randomized because all of the volunteers were similar in age.
The drug should not be approved, because trials of younger adults are never reliable.
The volunteers probably experienced a strong placebo effect.
The results may not show how the drug affects older adults, who could respond to it differently.
items.explain:
Paragraph 6 explains that “age, sex, and other factors can affect how a body responds to a drug,” so “results from a narrow group of volunteers may not apply to everyone.” Older adults, who often have arthritis and take many medicines, were left out, so the results may not apply to them.

A trial with a narrow age range can still be randomized. The passage does not say such trials are “never reliable,” and nothing suggests a stronger placebo effect in younger people.

items.prompt: According to the information sheet, how will it be decided whether a volunteer takes LX-7 or the placebo?
options: The volunteer will choose the group he or she prefers.
The study nurse will decide based on the volunteer’s health.
A computer will assign each volunteer to a group by chance.
Volunteers with the highest blood pressure will receive LX-7.
items.explain:
Under “What will happen?” the sheet says, “A computer will assign you by chance to one of two groups,” and each volunteer has “an equal chance of being placed in either group.”

The nurse reviews information with volunteers but does not choose groups, and neither the volunteer’s preference nor blood pressure level determines the group.

items.prompt: Based on the information sheet, which person would be eligible to join the study?
options: a 28-year-old man with high blood pressure who takes no medicines
a 64-year-old woman with high blood pressure who takes one blood pressure medicine
a 70-year-old man with high blood pressure who has kidney disease
a 55-year-old woman with high blood pressure who takes two blood pressure medicines
items.explain:
The 64-year-old woman meets every requirement: she is between 30 and 75, has been diagnosed with high blood pressure, and takes no more than one blood pressure medicine. Nothing says she is pregnant or has kidney disease.

The 28-year-old is too young, the 70-year-old has kidney disease, and the 55-year-old takes two blood pressure medicines, which is more than one.

items.prompt: The article “From Lab to Pharmacy” describes design features that protect a trial’s results from bias. Which features of Study LMR-214 are examples of those features? Select two answers.
options: A computer assigns each volunteer to a group by chance.
Neither the volunteers nor the study staff know who is taking LX-7.
Volunteers receive $50 for each completed clinic visit.
Volunteers check their blood pressure at home each morning.
Volunteers may leave the study at any time.
The study includes 6 clinic visits over 12 weeks.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 of the article names two protections against bias: random assignment (“a computer program assigns each participant to a group by chance”) and double-blinding (“neither the participants nor the researchers ... know who is receiving the real drug”). Study LMR-214 uses both.

The right to leave at any time protects volunteers (article paragraph 5), not the results. Payment, home monitoring, and the visit schedule are not discussed as protections against bias.

items.prompt: Using information from both the article and the information sheet, which phase of clinical trials is Study LMR-214 most likely to be?
options: Phase 2, because it enrolls a few hundred people who have the condition and follows an earlier safety study in a small group
Phase 1, because the information sheet describes possible side effects
Phase 3, because the study compares the medicine with a placebo
Phase 3, because the medicine has already been approved by the FDA
items.explain:
The sheet says about 240 adults with high blood pressure will take part, to learn whether LX-7 lowers blood pressure while watching for side effects, after “an earlier study in 60 healthy volunteers” checked safety. The article describes Phase 2 as enrolling “up to several hundred people who have the condition” to look for early signs the drug works. The earlier 60-person safety study matches Phase 1.

Every phase watches for side effects, so that does not make it Phase 1. Using a placebo alone does not make a study Phase 3, and the sheet states that LX-7 “has not been approved by the FDA.”

items.prompt: Paragraph 5 of the article explains that volunteers must give informed consent. Which detail from the information sheet most directly reflects this requirement?
options: About 240 adults will take part in the study.
Volunteers will receive $50 for each completed clinic visit, and parking is free.
The most common side effects in the earlier study were mild headaches and dizziness.
Before joining, a study nurse will go over the information with each volunteer, answer questions, and ask the volunteer to sign a consent form.
items.explain:
Informed consent means researchers explain the study and the person agrees before joining. The nurse reviewing the information, answering questions, and asking for a signed consent form is that process.

The number of participants and the payment are not part of consent. The side-effect information is something a volunteer should know, but the detail itself is about the earlier study’s results, not the consent process.

items.prompt: Why does the information sheet most likely include the statement “Taking part may or may not improve your blood pressure”?
options: to persuade volunteers that LX-7 does not work
to explain why volunteers must check their blood pressure at home
to make sure volunteers do not expect a guaranteed benefit, since some will receive a placebo and the medicine’s effect is not yet known
to warn volunteers that their blood pressure will rise during the study
items.explain:
Half the volunteers will take a placebo, and the purpose of the study is to find out whether LX-7 works. An honest information sheet must not promise benefits, which is part of explaining “possible risks and benefits” for informed consent (article paragraph 5).

The statement does not claim LX-7 fails, does not predict that blood pressure will rise, and is not connected to home monitoring.
